utterances.text: Well, amongst other things, there are more parameters and indicators that would lead us to be sure that they were the same speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Could you please read this intercept aloud, so that we can clarify some things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The complete conversation? "Hello, here I am. I've just called the boss. You have to talk over there and I will send a request to those up there in the ministry, and you can draft a request and hand it over to them on the spot. Only in the morning, I can't do anything now. In the morning, yes. For those and all others who are and you explain why, I'll mention the signed agreement this and that, and I will send it to them in the morning. "But who should I deliver it to? To the one over there. Well, I don't know at all whether I should go, because this one says, 'Colleague you came for nothing. I can neither help you nor can you solve it because the order'"-- then I cannot see to the extreme right whether it says "is", "as such." From whom? He says, "from the highest. " And, you know, I don't see anything behind the comma, probably says, "their highest is okay." "I'll ask them tomorrow to give us a list of those who were caught, and to turn them over according to the list with UNPROFOR escort and whoever else, because we need them to exchange for captured Serbs. Is that right? Okay."

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: You said the UNHCR, so can you please tell us what the abbreviation is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know each word literally, but it's the organisation of the United Nations that was in the region and that cared for the prisoners. I cannot be sure exactly what the abbreviation stands for, but the idea was for them to assist; that detained persons be freed or released or exchanged.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: There is a discrepancy in the original where it does say the "UNHCR" and the translation which says "UNPROFOR."

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: We would like to show you a document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Mrkic whether you were following, obviously you couldn't. But our attention has been drawn by the interpreters that there is a discrepancy between what appears in the fourth -- fifth line before the bottom in the B/C/S version, which is "UNHCR," and what appears in the fourth line from the bottom in the English version, which is "UNPROFOR." So the two are not the same. I don't think it's going to make much difference in any case because the question related to UNHCR in any case. But for the record, we need to point out that the English translation is not -- varies from the B/C/S text. And I thank the interpreters for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document 1378, that's the 65 ter list. The English version is A, and the Serbian version is B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Could you please read this intercept. If you read it, you will see that actually that's an introduction -- actually, rather, can you try to read it and then I will see if you agree with me that this conversation is actually the introduction to the conversations that we processed before, from which it is evident that Stevo and Ljubisa Beara are the speakers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2 of the Serbian version, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Do you see anywhere here, sir, Ljubisa Beara introducing himself, and do you see that Stevo from the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska directed him to Jeftic? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Since you've read all three intercepts, can you agree with me that the intercepts actually comprise one whole? By entity, I mean one processed topic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, we know what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Since you know what this about, then can you please tell us what it's about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the contents, you can see that it's pertaining to people who are escaping through Jezero, or actually from the lake or reservoir supplying the hydroelectric power station in Bajna Basta called called Perusac. And they're trying to escape to Serbia from Bosnia. They're fleeing the war, actually. Let me put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that the topic here is the exchange of prisoners of war with the assistance of international organisations, such as ICRC and UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, that's the topic as well. So this is the topic, and the other thing is the topic. I will agree with you that this is the topic discussed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this has to do with the exchange of prisoners of war, pursuant to lists that were supposed to be drawn by the ICRC with the assistance of the UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Mr. Mrkic. Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. As most of the questions have been put, I have no questions for this Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we see in e-court Exhibit 1158A from the 65 ter list. A is the English version, and B is the B/C/S version. We would like to be able to follow this simultaneously, and I will have only a couple of questions to the witness. Could we scroll down, the B/C/S version, all the way down to see -- yes, that's the conversation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, do you see this intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you turn off your mic, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please turn off your microphone. Yes, I can see the intercept. Would you give me some time, please, to go over it. I have read it, and as I said the other time, I even remember some of the details from this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that this is the intercept that you recorded yourself; you didn't receive it from the BH Army unit, which was at the same location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, let us turn to a portion of this conversation where the speaker marked with the letter M says - this is somewhere two-thirds into the conversation - he says, "We have to inform Mane up there." It says that "Mane is an employee of MUP, most likely an official." Do you see that portion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please read the next question and answer, and then answer my question. And my question is: Did you write down this notation in parentheses that Mane is an employee of MUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on what did you note down that "Mane is an employee of MUP, most likely a high official?"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that he was a MUP employee came from the following of what Milenko Zivanovic said, because he himself said that this had to do with the Public Security Centre in Zvornik. Now, as to why I wrote this down that he was most likely a high official, is that I concluded that he wasn't going to inform somebody who was not important; a beat officer, say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the next question and answer, it says the person marked with M, when he says, "Who should I inform?" And the answer is, "The Public Security Centre in Zvornik." Based on which you concluded, as you said, that Mane was a MUP employee and most likely a high official. My question is: Was your conclusion that Mane was an employee of Public Security Centre of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's based on the conversation. You can see that. It says there that Mane has police in Konjevic Polje and in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was the objective. There is another man here also named Mane, so I wanted to round this off. And to conclude, in the penultimate answer, once again, the person marked with M says, "Mane needs to do this for you because Mane has police in Konjevic Polje and Zvornik". Can we conclude that these were employees of police of the Public Security Centre, and that Mane was a high official who had power over them and could issue an order.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you know what they say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you shouldn't belabour this any further. I think he's told you, Mr. Stojanovic, on what basis he came to the conclusion as to who Mane was and he referred to this last paragraph before you even asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. There was just supplemental information here that he had police in Konjevic Polje; and since the answer to that was yes, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, since you have this document in front of you, I would like to ask you how you could conclude that one of the speakers was General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer in the same way as I did earlier. Milenko Zivanovic, just as other senior officers of the then army of Republika Srpska, did not call the other person, did not dial the other person himself. They would have other people do that for them. Well, all right. In this case, the Major identifies himself, and I'm sure that the identification was made after their subordinates had talked to each other. As I've already explained to you, this is how they worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So if I understand you properly, you say that in one part of the conversation that was not recorded or at least transcribed, somebody mentioned the name of General Ivanovic [as interpreted]. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said this to you. And what I said earlier, the telephones that were operational in this route, senior officials never directly answered the phone. No. Their subordinates would answer the phone and then they would be asked to put a certain person on the line, and we didn't note this down. We didn't record it, because sometimes these conversations would take a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like to correct the transcript, line 16. It's General Zivanovic, not Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau, for that. It will be accordingly corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, just above the transcript of this conversation you said that this was General Zivanovic. You also noted that he was the commander of the Drina Corps. Earlier on you said that you remembered bits of the conversation. Do you remember whether, in this conversation, you heard that General Zivanovic was the commander of the Drina Corps or is this an assumption that you made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not an assumption because General Milenko Zivanovic was the commander of the Drina Corps and we knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown page 1 of this document in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, can you see the date? The date is the 14th of July, 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: As to the conversation in which allegedly General Zivanovic participated was recorded on that very date. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the date is not indicated in the explanations, all of the conversations that follow below were made on that date. I didn't pay attention to that earlier. I didn't pay attention to whether there was a date or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You are absolutely sure that on the 14th of July, 1995, General Zivanovic was the Drina Corps commander on the basis of the conversation you were able to hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one did not hear that in the conversation. However, based on the information that we had at the time, most likely it was recorded then -- it was, rather, noted down then that he was the commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown Exhibit P2377; A for the English version and B for the B/C/S version. I'm indeed interested in the first conversation that was not translated into English. It's conversation 737 or 537. I don't think it exists in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, can you please have a look at this conversation that was recorded on the 11th of July, 1995? I'll give you enough time to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While the witness is reading the text, if questions are -- on the substance of this intercept are going to be made, on the assumption that it will also be tendered, we will need to have an English translation of it. Thank you. When you have finished reading it, Witness, please tell us. Okay. The witness is completed. Madam Fauveau, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, is it fair to say that in this conversation you heard that the two Dutch F-16 planes by mistake launched two bombs on the Muslims column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was the content of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Earlier on you stated on page 23 of today's transcript, that there were often mistakes, typos, as to dates in the work you did. Do you agree that today it's very hard to say which of the conversation is the fair translation of what you heard, what is the -- or what conversation contains mistakes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I feel very uncomfortable with the way the question has been phrased, at least basing myself on the interpretation. So if you could rephrase it again, I think it's not clear enough as it has been put to us in English anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I'm going to reformulate. It's not the interpreter's fault; I think it is mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Previously, you stated that there were mistakes made, errors, as to dates or typos, that sort of thing. Would you agree to say that today, 11 years or nearly 12 years after this conversation was recorded and transcribed, it is very hard to say which are the conversations where there are no errors to make a distinction between those and the conversation in which there are errors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say earlier that we made mistakes frequently; and as for the rest, yes, I would agree with you. It would be very difficult because one would need now to listen to all of the tapes and check to see perhaps there were some typing errors and erroneous dates, but I would fully agree with you that this is something that it would be very, very difficult to establish now. But, yes, it's possible, one could go over those conversations again.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it is possible to listen to the conversations again. So according to you, it is possible to establish which of the conversations are perfectly correct and without mistakes by listening to the tapes. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, my translation is missing the first part of the answer [sic] at page 54, line 20, so there is no misunderstanding. I don't know if that's the case with anybody else's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] What we have here is a problem with -- if you look at line 21, you see that the previous translation continues. So I take it that it should be read, but yes it's possible one could go over these conversations again. And line 21, "It is possible to listen to the conversations again. So according to you, it is possible to establish which of the conversations are perfectly correct and without mistakes by listening to the tapes. Is that so?" I think it's clear enough. I don't -- although there is this indication that the previous translation continues, sort of indicating that there is an interruption, I don't really think there is an interruption. That's -- that's how I read it. If I am not correct, please, I stand to be corrected. Does my explanation satisfy you, Mr. Thayer, or not? If you think there is still something missing, please speak out.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My only concern, Your Honour, is whether the question as intended refers to tape recordings of all the conversations or just some of the conversations. Because of that missing portion, I'm not sure if that was expressed or intended or not. There is an issue as to whether all of the conversation were record or not or whether we have in our possession tape recordings of all the conversations. I just didn't want that to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that. Madam Fauveau, could you address that, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, did you mean to say that indeed it is today possible to establish the accuracy of the conversations only by listening to the tape recordings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the listening of the recordings, it is my belief that it is possible to establish the accuracy of these conversations that were transcribed. Yes, that can be established. As for the other things we noted down, the information about the speakers, I don't know whether recordings of that still exist. And it is possible that they exist, but have not been transcribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the question, I don't think you address the most important word or phrase in Madam Fauveau's question; namely, that the only way, the only way of establishing the accuracy of the conversations of the intercepts is by listening to tape recordings. My question is: If there are no tape recordings but there are records of intercepts, would it follow that the absence of tape recordings one cannot establish the accuracy of those recorded intercepts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, naturally, if we have the recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But if you don't have a recording, can you still establish the accuracy of an intercept or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be established if there is no recording based on the events that transpired on the ground later on. I think that all of us are aware of what happened afterwards. All of these events that took place showed. When I said that it is impossible to establish precisely, I was referring to mistakes in certain words, not to the topic in general; the topic of the conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, I do understand that what you are refer to. But say if the name of the speaker or the date is not accurate, would you agree with me in saying that this could change the meaning of the conversations totally -- of a conversation totally?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need the witness to affirm or deny that. We all know it, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. The Pandurevic team had indicated that you have no cross-examination, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: We have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have covered everyone. Is there re-examination, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we have P02377 displayed, I believe that is the intercept dated July 11th, 1995, that my learned colleague, Madam Fauveau, displayed a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we don't an English translation available, so I just ask you if you could read what the introductory portion of that intercept says underneath where it says "Report Number 537."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I read it out loud?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you would, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the said day following or monitoring the radio relay route Pale, frequency 836, at 1555 hours, we registered the conversation between journalist Bora, from the Serbska Vojska magazine and a certain journalist Milan from Serbia. We heard only Bora whose interesting comments were as follows."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I just had one other question, and this came up as a result of the question that the Honourable Judge Kwon had the other day. You and I haven't had a chance to discuss this, so I am just going to ask you whether you can describe for the Trial Chamber the method by which your reports were physically transmitted to your command once they were transcribed, encoded, and sent off. And I understand that you were working with one agency, and there were other agencies at your site; but if you could first speak to what your agency's procedure was and, if you know, the procedure for the other entities, if you could describe that as well. I don't want to you speculate. But if you have that knowledge, could you share that with the Trial Chamber while you are here, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon, and then, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can my colleague give us a reference as to when this question was asked by Judge Kwon, because I am not sure that exactly this question refers to something that was mentioned. I think it goes beyond the scope of what was mentioned in the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully associate myself with what Mr. Bourgon has just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We also believe that our colleagues are correct in this objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm almost tempted to ask Judge Kwon. But...

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have the cite here. It is on page 7231. The question from -- from His Honour Judge Kwon is: "I have a brief question to the witness. I'm not sure whether this is an appropriate question to put to you," and this was the prior witness, "but I wonder if you know by any chance the method how typed versions or encrypted versions of the intercepts were sent to Tusla or command?" So I am just using the opportunity now that we have go somebody here, so we don't need to possibly call somebody back if he has the answer to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question may be why you did not deal with it during your direct; then maybe the question, the Defence may put.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes. It is beyond the scope of the direct, and also he is talking now about a witness before this witness, so he misrepresented. He said it was this witness you asked a question to a week ago Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If it please the Court, we're simply trying to assist the Court with a witness who is here. If the Court wishes not to listen to the testimony, then we can call it a day. I just thought if he can help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I appreciate Mr. Thayer's assistance. He meant to assist the Chamber, so I would like to put that question as a Chamber's question. Mr. Witness, could you answer that question put by Mr. Thayer as to the method how the typed, encrypted version actually sent to your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can answer that. After entering the transcripts into the computer, the conversations or the material was encrypted; then it was sent to our, as you call it, command. It was a headquarters or a seat, but let's call it a command. In two ways, we used to send it. If the telephone lines were all right with the seat, we would then do it through a modem connection. After encryption the communication was sent via a special programme for communication between two computers. It was sent to our seat. The second way was if we did not have a telephone connection, because of various electricity cuts - sometimes the telecom or the PTT system at the time would be inoperative - then we would use the packet radio connection. Do I need to explain the Paket radio? I can do that, but in short it's the same way of communication, but it proceeds via radio equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The first method would be something similar to a secret e-mail, if you can say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, the first method was a computer modem connection. It's used today as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was whether it was a secure question or not, I suppose, what Judge Kwon wanted to ask you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, of course. If you are thinking of the security of the information, of the data, yes, I emphasise that. The data was encrypted; before that it was protected by a certain data encryption programme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any further questions on redirect, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We don't have any further questions for you, sir, which means you are free to go. Before you leave the courtroom, however, I wish to thank you on behalf of the Tribunal and my colleagues for having come over to give evidence in this case. You will receive all the assistance you require to facilitate your return back home. And before you leave we wish you a safe journey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and best wishes to you also. Thank you for inviting me and for making it possible for me to present my view and to contribute to the struggle to prove the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we come to the documents. I think we can draw the curtains up again. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, logically, in my submission, the Court should hear Mr. Bourgon's response to the Prosecution motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm coming to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because we do oppose a number of these exhibits, but for different reasons to those contained in the motion, so to speak. I haven't made that very clear. It will become clear in a moment after my learned friend has addressed the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take your advice, Mr. Josse, and we invite Mr. Bourgon to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, in light of the rulings issued thus far by the Trial Chamber in respect of Prosecution requests to amend its Rule 65 ter list of proposed exhibits and with a view to protecting the rights of the accused for appeal purposes, we oppose the Prosecution motion, and I will endeavour to explain why in as few words as possible. Mr. President, the basic argument that is always put forward by the Prosecution in such requests is that the material has been in the possession of the Defence for some time and that, therefore, for this reason there would be no prejudice. The fact of the matter is, Mr. President, that on the EDS, the Electronic Disclosure System, there are more than one million pages that have been disclosed to the Defence on that system. If we compare this with the Rule 65 ter list of proposed exhibits, it contains 2.000 exhibits and some 10.000 pages of material. That leaves, Mr. President, some 990.000 pages which the Prosecution has made available to the Defence, but which the Prosecution has expressly did not include as part of its case against the accused. I say "made available," Mr. President, because the word "disclosure" simply cannot be used here. These 990.000 pages which were placed on the EDS and which was given to the Defence along with lists of generic nature without any specific references to either witnesses or issues in the indictment. What we respectfully submit, Mr. President, is that what must be borne in mind is that those documents which are listed on the list that the Defence receives, they're not readily available. Each of these documents must literally be found on the electronic disclosure system. And sometimes we wonder whether anyone has actually attempted to go on what is called the EDS to basically experience what we, as Defence counsel, experience when we try to find this material on generic lists that we receive. Sometimes, we mentioned this a long time ago, it can take up to 15 minutes to locate one document on the Electronic Disclosure System. The difference here, Mr. President, is that the Prosecution has both unlimited resources at its disposal and that it has had more than 12 years and two full trials to put its case together. The Defence on the other side has both limited resources and we have had limited time to try and understand the Prosecution's case and to try and prepare the case for the Defence. It all comes down to the purpose of Rule 65 ter, which was adopted by the Honourable Judges of this Tribunal for a reason. That reason, Mr. President, the Defence respectfully submits, that it is to allow the accused to know the case they have to meet before trial proceedings get under way. There are reasons for this, Mr. President, and we feel that sometimes by looking only at the timing upon which these documents have been released that we fail to look at the object and purpose of Rule 65 ter, which includes, first of all, the need for trial proceedings to proceed in accordance with the set and established rules that will be respected. Secondly, the need to avoid taking the accused by surprise. Thirdly, the need for the accused to be able to investigate in relation to documents which it is put on notice that the Prosecution will be using at trial. Fourthly, the need for the accused to prepare its defence on the basis of those documents which we know will be used. And fifthly, and more importantly, because the Trial Chamber and this Tribunal both attach a lot of importance to proceeding swiftly, it's to avoid interruptions in trial proceedings by having enterless requests to add additional documents. We respectfully submit, Mr. President, that the position adopted so far by the Trial Chamber does not take into account the object and purpose of allowing the accused to know the case they have to meet before trial proceedings get underway. The Trial Chamber has previously held that the Prosecution would have to show good cause before documents could be added to its Rule 65 ter list of proposed exhibits. In this case, the Prosecution puts in its motion that these documents are the result of an oversight. First, of course, they say that the documents have been in the possession of the Defence for a long time. That's an argument that is reiterated in every single motion. But the Prosecution motion does not say that it does -- it confirms on the other hand that no notice has been given to the Defence that these documents will be used in the trial; and then the Prosecution argues that they are a result of an oversight. Obviously, Mr. President, oversight is not the first oversight from the Prosecution, nor is it the last, as it appears; but more importantly, oversight, in our respectful opinion, does not meet the good-cause criteria. Furthermore, we submit that considering the resources available to the Prosecution, considering the number of years the Prosecution has had to prepare its case and that it has been working on these events, and the time periods that these documents have been in its possession, that oversight is simply an unacceptable justification to add and modify its Rule 65 ter rule of -- list of exhibits. It is a known principle, Mr. President, that the Prosecution is independent and that the Prosecution is a master of its own case. We don't discuss that. Prosecution independently decides which documents it is going to use at trial and which witnesses will be called. However, Mr. President, it is also a very known principle that once the Prosecution makes its bed, it must sleep in it. In our view, Mr. President, the Prosecution cannot keep adding more documents to its list by oversight without the Trial Chamber stepping in and putting an end to such request with a view to protecting the rights of the accused in accordance with Article 20 of the Statute. Turning to the specifics of the Prosecution motion, our position is as follows: Firstly, with respect to Witness PW-105, we object to all five documents. Let me address the first three, documents A, B and C. Document A is a 15 July hospital records. Document C is an ICRC notice along with a picture bearing number 8144. Both of these documents were disclosed to the Defence for the first time on 21 November 2006. Mr. President, we would have objected then, and it is not because the testimony of this witness was delayed or postponed that we would not object now for the exact same reason. The delay in postponing the testimony of that witness does not cure the fact that this material has been in the procession of the Prosecution for a long time, and it falls into the oversight category. Document B, same arguments hold for these -- for this document; in addition to the fact that it was not even disclosed to us on 21 November, as were documents A and C. As for document D, which is a montage of four family photos, which was given to the Prosecution by the witness. First of all, the Prosecution has had the opportunity of meeting with this witness on many occasions. There is no reason why this material could not be made available sooner to the Defence. Moreover, this material, the four family pictures, the Defence fails to see how this is relevant or it can add any probative value to the testimony of Witness 101. And, of course, this begs the question once again: How long has this material been in the possession of the Defence [sic], which is not mentioned in the motion. As for the photography of the wounds, these refer to documents bearing number 8713 to 8717. These documents were disclosed with the motion on Friday. Again, the question is: How long have these documents been in the possession of the Prosecution, and the motion itself at paragraph 6 specifies and confirms that the Prosecution decided this week to add new documents to its list because of the level of contestation or degree to which its case is being contested by the Defence. There are ways in the rules for the Prosecution to improve its case or to do a rebuttal if it believes that we are contesting more than what was anticipated. But the question is, these documents were not disclosed previously and it was the Prosecution's choice whether to disclose or not to disclose these documents. With respect to Witness PW-145, there are three intercepts. The first two dates from 11 July and from 12 July. According to the Prosecution motion, they believe that these documents were included in the authentification binder of witness Stefanie Frease, but they realise this week that they are not; another oversight. To use the words of my colleague on the other side, intercepts have been around forever. That is what my colleague likes to use whenever we raise any arguments in respect to intercepts. The Prosecution will then argue that they are adding intercepts because or as a result of the Trial Chamber decision. We respectfully submit, Mr. President, that the Trial Chamber's decision, which goes back to -- I don't have the exact date, I think it's September or October, cannot be a blanket authorisation to keep adding intercepts until the end of the trial. At some point this has got to stop. Once again, the oversight of not adding these documents, we believe must be sanctioned in order to protect the rights of the accused. As for the 10th of July intercept, the third document, the Prosecution adds that because this document was already used with Witness PW-144, that this would be sufficient to say, Well, let's use it again. We submit, Mr. Prosecutor [sic], that this is not an additional reason why this document should be added to the Rule 65 ter list of exhibits. In conclusion, Mr. President, we ask you to deny the Prosecution motion; and moreover with respect to avoiding any further delays which can be attributed to Prosecution motions to amend its Rule 65 ter list of proposed exhibits, we believe that the time limit should be imposed and it should not be longer than 14 days for the Prosecution to cure and correct its case and to stop filing motions due to oversight to add documents over and over again. We reiterate, Mr. President, that this case has been prepared on the basis of some 2.000 exhibits which were put in the Prosecution's list. If we simply look at the number -- the numbering of the list today, we believe we are at 2.244 documents. Now, they are not all due to changes in the Rule 65 ter list, some of these documents are simply pseudonym sheets, that is recognised. But it just shows the extent to which we are constantly being faced, being presented with new documents which constantly keeps the Defence off balance and does not allow us to protect the rights of the accused. At some point, Mr. President, a stop must be put to the Prosecution so they can present their case and we can proceed and go swiftly with this trial. Respectfully submitted. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. I just would like you to make one thing clear. Is it your suggestion that if there has been an oversight on the part of the Prosecution, then the door is completely closed for further discussion or whether there is or there can be a good cause for allowing these documents to be included in the list? Is this what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In part, yes, Mr. President. But we go back to what we said previously. It is not -- there are -- there can be exceptions or there can be instances in which a document will be so relevant which has such a high probative value that the oversight can be cured by the fact that this is something that really must be added to the case. The case cannot proceed because it is a document that will make a difference between guilty and not guilty. And we argued this previously. The probative value is important, and why is it that this oversight was committed? Now, we use the word "oversight," but it goes beyond oversight. The real reason is they have these documents, they have the resources, they have the time, they have the personnel, and they keep adding these documents on and on. We figure that this, Mr. President, at this point, unless they can come up with a document that is absolutely critical to its case, then these motions must be denied. Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I have -- my colleagues my want to add that these submissions which are specifically addressed on behalf of the accused Nikolic, but my colleagues may want to intervene. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We should have had our break five minutes ago. So my suggestion that we will have the break now and then any further submissions from the Defence teams and reply or response from Mr. Thayer and we can decide the matter. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Zivanovic. I understand, because I had notice, Mr. Meek is standing up, wishing to address the Trial Chamber on the issues that we were dealing with before. I think Mr. Dunjic can wait. You will introduce him when appropriate, and we can proceed with the submissions. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just very briefly, I want to adopt of course the arguments made by Mr. Bourgon. Further, I would just point out to the Court that we believe oversight never equates to good cause, and it never should in any court, let alone a criminal court -- a criminal trial like this, if we keep allowing or if Your Honours keep allowing the OTP to continue in this manner, and I've said it before and God willing, I wouldn't have to say it again, but this is turning into a trial by ambush. We can see on the horizon by motions, submissions filed by the Prosecution, that there will shortly be this issue arising over some six witnesses that by oversight they forgot to add to their list. We just ask that this stop. It is not proper, and it is prejudicing our clients and our case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Meek. Does anyone else wish to make further submissions? Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we also oppose the Prosecution motion. When the Court has determined whether to allow the motion or not -- let me start again. If the Court allows the motion, then we have further submissions in relation to exhibits pertaining to the last witness, but they are is separate matter to this motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, but we are coming to those as well, basically. Any further submissions? Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would also like to tell the Chamber that we join the submissions of Mr. Bourgon, and I would like to inform the Chamber that Mr. Dunjic is present and he is on my right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I need to slow you down, even stop you, because we are not receiving interpretation. Can you start again, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We still don't have interpretation. Basically, I'm almost going to interpret myself. She said that the Defence for General Miletic doesn't have any particular objection or problems with admitting the documents which the Prosecution is seeking to admit -- not admit, to have included in the -- yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If I can just correct you slightly, Mr. President. We didn't have any particular position, but we are joining the very persuasive ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Out of sympathy, sympathy support. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It's a little bit more. It is a matter of principle, and we are joining the arguments of Nikolic and Beara Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Any further remarks? None.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I was just going to say the documents are of no concern to us, but we do support the matters-- principle advanced by Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, pretty much the same position as Madam Fauveau. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Likewise, given what Mr. Bourgon said, we join in and the other Defence teams have supported the argument as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Mr. Thayer, are you in a position to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Let me begin by focusing directly on the exhibits that are at issue with respect to the witness who just finished testifying. What we are talking about are two intercepts, which were included in the packet that Defence counsel has had for some time now. There is no surprise, no ambush, no 999.000 other documents that my learned colleagues have to fish through to find these documents. They have been made available through the procedure that we have been pursuing since we began the testimony of the intercept operators by providing each and every intercept that we intend to use to Defence counsel well in advance of their testimony. That is what was done in this case, Your Honours, with respect to the intercepts at issue. The only problem we had was we were under the mistaken understanding that two of these intercepts, which were provided in great detail to Defence counsel, did not have the 65 ter number we thought they did. We explained that in the motion - I won't belabour that point with the Trial Chamber - but that is what we are talking about. This is not a case of new evidence, a changing theory, or anything else that Defence counsel has not been aware of with respect to this particular witness and these particular intercepts for some time. I just want to make that clear so we understand that is not about ambushing or this not about trial by surprise. We have supplied in addition to those actual intercepts a summary of the intercepts, the users of the intercepts. All of this information is provided pursuant to the mechanism that the Trial Chamber has set up and that we have been pursuing, and there will be mistakes. There will be oversights. These were oversights. I can't promise, and I would never promise that there not be oversights in the future. I think I can almost promise that there will be oversights in the future, as one can naturally expect in a multi-defendant, complex case like the one in which we are involved now. These seven accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's nice music for Mr. Bourgon's ears.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just want to be as up front as I can on that larger issue, Your Honour. However, these seven accused have not stood trial before. This is not the same case that has been prosecuted previously in terms of the Srebrenica events. There is new evidence that has been developed in the course of this particular investigation. We are dealing with that new evidence. We have, I think, done as good a job as humanly possible thus far. Have we fallen short? We have fallen short of that goal of perfection and no oversights, absolutely. Do we like it? No. Does providing this relevant evidence to the Court, be it these intercepts on which the Defence counsel and the accused have been on notice for some time or photographs of a survivor's victims or of his family members about which we expect there to be testimony, or himself which shows the age of which these events occurred. Are those relevant? Are they ultimately in pursuit of the truth-finding mission of this Tribunal? Yes, Your Honours. Again, we are doing our best with respect to making these materials available. With respect to the medical records, for example to which my learned colleague referred, those specific medical records identified by ERN were placed on the exhibit list for the Prosecution's list of witnesses back in October, actually, when we thought these two witnesses, PW-101 and 105, were scheduled to testify at that time. The actual documents were subsequently disclosed, that was some months ago. Those two witnesses' testimony was thereafter postponed at the request of Defence counsel, and then we entered the intercept heaven that we've been in for the last several months. Now that we are again enjoined in preparing for these two witnesses' testimony, we realised that these documents, which the Defence counsel already had notice of, did not have 65 ter numbers. With respect to the two remaining items, Your Honours, that did not -- that were not disclosed to Defence counsel, again, one is a montage of photographs that I believe were mistakenly left off the initial exhibit list back in November because it looked like it was a duplicate exhibit. The montage actually includes one of the photographs that was disclosed and listed on the exhibit list back in November. I believe that is why the montage didn't make it on to the list. Again, it is an oversight, but is far from trial by ambush. It is evidence that is consistent with the OTP witness statement that the Defence was also provided some months ago. Finally, Your Honours, with respect to the wound photographs, as we explained, these are photographs that we've only recently decided need to be brought to the Trial Chamber's attention. We would prefer that they not be. I have endeavoured to secure a stipulation. I have heard back from a couple of my learned colleagues, and I'm optimistic so far, although I need to touch base with everyone else. Again, these are photographs that are referred to in the witness' OTP statements, which was disclosed to the Defence some months ago. Again, this is not a matter of surprise. It is a matter of oversight? It is a matter of time consuming argument? Absolutely. Again, though, it is a matter of providing this relevant evidence to the Trial Chamber to present the fullest picture, the most complete accounting we can of these crimes in pursuit of the truth in this Tribunal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Does anyone wish to add anything? Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. President. Simply to say the Prosecution has decided to lead some witnesses in this case. One of those witnesses is a victim who was injured in a particular way and, of course, we've been aware that this witness was coming to testify. Now, I don't know if the Prosecution expected the Defence to simply sit down and not to say anything, and just listen to the testimony and not contest the testimony. But in our view, Mr. President, it is a basic procedure that-- if you're going to lead a victim that was hurt in a particular way, you think about medical records, you think about pictures of wounds, and that is simply part of the basic package that goes with leading a victim as witness. Now, to decide this at this point in time because they suddenly face more opposition than they expected, simply it defeats the purpose of the Rule 65 ter. That's my conclusion. It all comes down to: Is there an object and a purpose behind this rule when this rule was put together by the Judges? We don't have access to the discussions that took place amongst the Plenary of Judges when this rule was put together, but there was an object and a purpose. There was a reason, and we believe that we are defeating the object and purpose of this rule by allowing continuous requests for additional documents. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. I do have comments two make, if I could just make in response to, in reply to what my learned friend said must moments ago. On page 74, lines 2 and 3, he states that "these seven accused have not stood trial before." We are contesting that, as we have in our opening statements. In the Blagojevic case, the Prosecution defended Mr. Beara, and now they are taking an inconsistent position. We will be filing a motion in due course, when it is right, on the substantive and procedural aspects that, so they cannot take such inconsistent theories. I just don't want that to be left without a comment from our side. On the second point, the Prosecution somewhat refreshingly tells us on the next line on the same page 74, lines 3 and 4, that this is not the same case. It is the same facts, Your Honour. But if it's not the same case, then perhaps the Prosecutor will refrain from always relying on those judgements on issue, such as whether the intercepts should be admissable or not. And my point is they are again taking an inconsistent position. What we are looking for is guidance from the Trial Chamber. I disagree with him that it is not trial by ambush. When they bring new evidence in, regardless of whether it is directly against our client or my accused or against any of the others, they are prohibited by the rules to do so without leave of Court. To say that it is an oversight, is certainly not just cause in any courtroom, in my view, respectfully. To suggest that they're going bring in six other witnesses that they now deem to be as, Mr. Meek State stated, "important," that should have been done years before. It's not a question of whether you're trying one accused; it's a question of the facts. The Srebrenica facts, as we've seen from the multiple witnesses if not 90 per cent of the witnesses, they've testified previously. If we're going to try the case in a vacuum, then that should be the Court's ruling. Now, we can shortcut this case, but I know that that is not the intent of this Tribunal, I know that it is not the intent of this Trial Chamber to do so. We request and submit that the Prosecutor's motion be rejected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Just for clarification, in respect to the three intercepts -- two intercepts relating to the last witness that we had, am I right in stating that these are not included as yet in the list of Prosecution exhibits or are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, they are included in the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you indicate them, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. They are exhibit -- the exhibit located at tab number 3, it was a given the 65 ter number of 1074; that is the 11 July 1995 conversation at 1645 on about which the witness was questioned at length by Defence counsel. The second one is at tab 10; that is a 12 July 1995 conversation recorded at 1845 hours. We did not lead any evidence concerning that intercept, Your Honour. And if I may just add one minor point, Mr. President. As I just answered the Court's question, I think one thing we also need to look at, and this has been one of the touch stones of the Court's decisions thus far with respect to the 65 ter applications, is when the Court conducts its balance, it has been very careful to weigh very heavily the rights of the accused in making its determination. And I think what we've seen time and again with any of these exhibits, which have been the subject of the 65 ter motions, is that counsel has ample opportunity to prepare. They do obviously prepare because as we just saw with on of these two exhibits, there was substantial cross-examination of the witness concerning one of them. And I think that we are proceeding along the very deliberate course, time consuming perhaps, but it is one that ultimately preserves the rights of the accused and moves forward in pursuit of the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Now, gentlemen, as regards the rest of the Prosecution exhibits, and, of course, without prejudice to what has been submitted in relation to those two that have already been dealt with, are there any objections? Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we object to the intercept that is found in tab 2, as well as the intercept that is found in tab 3. And just to reiterate, the one in tab 3 is the one that is problematical in any event, that has apparently been given 65 ter number 1074; but that, it turns out, is some sort of phantom number and hasn't yet been given a number, subject to a decision on the motion that the Court has just heard argument about. Your Honour, the reason we oppose the admission into evidence of these two intercepts is we contend that they do not reflect what is actually contained on the tape, which is the best evidence that is available. In a few moments' time, we're going to invite the Court to admit into evidence 6D14 and 6D15, which are the transcripts prepared by the Prosecution of the actual tapes of those two conversations. And we submit that the Court should introduce into evidence 6D14 and 6D15 really on the best evidence principle, because those are the tapes. The tapes exist in this particular case. They have been played for the Court. The witness accepted their veracity. It is a transcript of the tapes, rather than the other two documents, the two in the tabs, that we submit should be admitted into evidence. That's our contention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse. Any further objections to the admissibility or admission of the other documents which the Prosecution is seeking to tender? So there are none. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just two points. One is the -- I think the practice with these particular operators from this particular unit has been to place the intercepts under seal because there are code identifiers on the documents, and we just ask that that be done with respect to all of the intercept exhibits that are listed here. I also would like to correct a typographical error at Exhibit 1190C; again, that should be 1190B, for the record. If I might briefly respond to my learned colleague's objection to tabs 2 and 3. We would welcome the introduction of the those tape recordings as well as the transcript. But they should come in so that the Court can compare them with the printout about which this witness testified, so that in making its assessment of the reliability and authenticity of these intercepts, which is a great part of the effort that we're undertaking here, the Court has all that information and can compare them side by side and see how accurately these intercept operators got their job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the position is, as I see it, is the following, and correct me if I'm wrong: The intercept behind tab 3 and the intercept behind tab 10, the decision on those two intercepts arising or in the wake of the Prosecution motion of last Friday will be handed down by us tomorrow morning. That of course is without prejudice to your further submission in relation to the first of these two. Now, that leaves only the intercept behind tab 2 and potentially the same intercept behind tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's not the same, Your Honour. They are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. They are not the same. They are two different ones. But what I mean to say is that, basically, we are left with the intercepts behind tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is contested by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the same intercept we spoke of before that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- behind tab 3, which is also objected on a different, separate ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest to my colleagues that we leave this also for tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I mention one other matter in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course, perhaps we could turn to those exhibits the Defence would like to introduce through PW-145, if I may jump to that now. A list has been provided to the Registrar. The Chamber will see that that includes 6D14 and 6D15. Of course, all of these documents; that is, 6D14 and 6D15, tabs 2 and 3, are dependent to some extent on the Court's ruling in relation to intercepts in general. I make that observation because it's perhaps the first occasion that the -- a Defence team have provided a rival transcript, if I can call it that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Josse. So we'll decide on these three intercepts tomorrow morning. That's the one behind tab 2, the one behind tab 3, on a dual approach, and the one behind tab 10. The rest is as follows: Not having heard any objections, that's premised. First off, the documents to be tendered, that's the OTP witness statement dated 7 February 2007, is admitted, and will be served under seal. The pseudonym will also be under seal. All the other intercepts except, the ones that I referred to in regard to which our decision is postponed, are marked for identification as per our previous ruling. All right. Now we come to the documents that the Gvero Defence team who like to tender. We'll take them one by one. The first one is the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska dated the 14th March of 1995. It's marked as 65 ter number 6D7. Is there any objection, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it is admitted. Then there are the two transcripts from the tape, 6D14, 6D15, to which Mr. Josse has referred.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, no objection to those transcripts. I was alerted to my learned friend's reference to a rival transcript. I believe it is the practice that include we the transcripts of the audio tapes, along with the transcripts of the printouts; and just as long as one doesn't supplant the other, that would be our position, consistent with my prior position, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So our decision on 6D14 and 15 will be taken tomorrow when we decide on the rest. And there is an intercept, 6D21, what's that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's the one that was put to the witness by Mr. Krgovic, and it is an intercept between our client and Mr. Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it is admitted. And, again, it will be marked for identification purposes like all the other intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then there is another one, intercept Gvero/Koljevic, 6D43.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Again, it was put to the witness, and it's there for similar illustrative purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't have a translation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's not yet been translated, and it will need to be marked for identification in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be marked for identification, not necessarily upgraded upon translation. It will remain marked for identification until we have handed our final decision on the admissibility of intercepts. Madam Fauveau, you had -- you made use of one transcript, it's 547 or something like that. Do you wish to tender it or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Translation. Again, we haven't received interpretation. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like for the time being if the document could be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's mark it for identification and please, Prosecution, procure us a translation thereof. It needs to be given a number, which would be what? 5D ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It will be 5D188.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. So I think we have concluded this chapter, with all due apologies to Mr. Elderkin. I suggest that we bring in the witness and at least we can explain to him why he has been kept waiting, and we can start him off and then we will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome. You are about to start giving evidence. Our rules require that you enter a solemn declaration with us that you will be speaking the truth. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of the solemn declaration. Please read it out and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable. I owe you, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, an explanation why you have been waiting outside to start before you could start giving evidence. We had another witness and then we had some lengthy procedural problems to -- issues to deal with, which has taken us all this time. Mr. Elderkin will be examining you in chief, starting today, and then we will proceed tomorrow. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, good afternoon, Your Honours. I only have in fact very few questions, so given the time I may not succeed to put all of them today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could I first ask you to say your name, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK.
utterances.text: John Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, Dr. Clark, what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK.
utterances.text: I'm a forensic pathologist based in the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And how long have you been a pathologist?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK.
utterances.text: I've been a forensic pathologist about 22 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And could you tell us a bit about your professional qualifications in that field?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK.
utterances.text: Well, I'm a medical doctor, so I have basic medical qualifications. I am also trained as a pathologist and have the qualification in that, and I have a specialist qualification in the forensic medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And where are you working at the moment?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK.
utterances.text: I am based at the University of Glasgow in Scotland.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And what does your job involve basically, day to day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK.
utterances.text: Two things. Primarily carrying out post-mortem examinations, medical/legal post-mortem examinations for the legal authorities in that region. Last year, not the current, I did 600 post-mortems, 600 autopsies last year and that's about an average year. I also, being -- based at the university, there is a teaching commitment to undergraduate, post-graduates; and I am also, as a head of the forensic pathologist services, there are administrative duties to do as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can, I would now like to ask about the work you did in Bosnia, just start by asking what -- when was that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK.
utterances.text: The main work was in 1999, 2000, 2001, when I was the chief pathologist for the mortuary operations there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Who was that you were working for?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK.
utterances.text: That was the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What was the purpose of your work?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK.
utterances.text: This was to look at the bodies which had been taken from the grave sites by the field team, to look at them and primarily to identify injuries on the bodies and try and establish causes of death. In between times, we also tried to assist with identification and retrieval of evidence, any other evidence on the bodies, but primarily we were there to establish cause of death by looking at the injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And what were your specific tasks as chief pathologist?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK.
utterances.text: Well, as long as -- as well as being a pathologist carrying out the post-mortems, I did as many as anyone, it was my responsibility to oversee the whole operations; really oversee the whole operations of the mortuary not just the pathologist, but the anthropologists, photographs, et cetera, and make sure there was a system, correct system of working and just -- and coordinate all the findings at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you say which were the specific grave sites that you worked on during that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK.
utterances.text: Well, the ones related to Srebrenica, because there were other grave sites, but I am presuming you just want the Srebrenica sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK.
utterances.text: Well, in 1999 we involved in Kozluk, Konjevic Polje, and Nova Kasaba, and part of Glogova. The following year we did Lazete and again Glogova; and the final year, 2001, Glogova, Ravnice, and Zeleni Jadar. We have also done some of Ravnice in 2000, but these were the grave sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And among your team, were you working only with pathologist?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK.
utterances.text: No. Usually, at any one time, there were three pathologist in the mortuary. There were an equal number of anthropologist, then there was support staff of scenes of crime officers, photographer, radiographer, secretaries. So it was quite a big team.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And could you briefly explain the difference between the work of the pathologists and the work of the anthropologists?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK.
utterances.text: The pathologists' role in this work, and as at work in the normal practice, is to try and establish cause of death. Their expertise is in looking at soft tissues, looking for diseases, injuries, et cetera. The anthropologist' expertise is related to the bones, the bony skeleton, and they have no expertise in looking at the soft tissues, which surround the skeleton. But they have a particular expertise in that, both in terms of trying to use the skeleton to identify a person and also in assisting in interpretation of injuries to the skeleton. So because of the nature of the bodies we were dealing with, there was a very close liaison between the pathologist and anthropologies, and we worked closely together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see on the clock that there is only one minute remaining, and I have perhaps five more minutes worth of questions. At any rate, I don't know whether you would like me to start on Dr. Clark's reports or just keep that as a short block to start tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can start tomorrow morning. We wouldn't like to keep the other Chamber waiting. So Dr. Clark we'll see you again tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 20th day of February, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
